live.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
live.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL: a threat actor tracked under many names
live.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for an actor also known as Kimsuky and APT43. The catalogue lists its aliases and tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the name Secureworks uses for this threat actor.
Other vendors track it under many other names, including APT43, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, THALLIUM, TA427 and Black Banshee.
The catalogue lists eight tools tied to the actor: BabyShark, FastFire, FastSpy, FireViewer, KONNI, KimJongRAT, Kimsuky and ReconShark.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
next.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL, also tracked as Kimsuky: phishing-led intrusions, mostly aimed at South Korea
next.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is tracked under many names, chiefly Kimsuky. Reports describe spear-phishing, fake installers and mobile spyware, mostly aimed at South Korean targets. Several sources attribute the activity to North Korea.

sentences.t: The catalogue lists many aliases for NICKEL KIMBALL, including Kimsuky, APT43, THALLIUM, Velvet Chollima, Emerald Sleet and Black Banshee.
BleepingComputer, reporting on Microsoft's findings, calls Kimsuky a North Korean state actor, also known as Emerald Sleet or Velvet Chollima.
Breakglass Intelligence attributes a Kimsuky command server it analysed to the DPRK, with high confidence.
Sekoia and Kudelski Security report that some DPRK experts regard Kimsuky as a mega-cluster of several branches, such as TA406 and TA408.

Genians says KONNI overlaps with Kimsuky and APT37 in targets and infrastructure, so some researchers class them as one group. It cites the MSMT report, which assesses Kimsuky and KONNI as distinct groups.
Microsoft says Kimsuky used ClickFix-style tactics in limited attacks since January 2025, aimed at people in international affairs groups, NGOs, government agencies and media companies.
Genians assesses with moderate confidence that a 2026 campaign against South Korean policy and security professionals was Kimsuky's work.
South Korea's National Police Agency said Kimsuky exploited an email server flaw at a defense subcontractor between April and July 2023.
AhnLab reported signs in July 2022 that AppleSeed, a backdoor it says Kimsuky mainly uses, was being spread to maintenance contractors of a military unit.

South Korean officials said hackers believed to be operating from North Korea breached the nuclear research body KAERI through a VPN flaw. One of thirteen IP addresses involved was linked to infrastructure used by Kimsuky.
Breakglass Intelligence describes tax-themed and Naver-themed phishing lures aimed at South Korean users, tied to the Kimsuky server it analysed.

A January 2021 report on ESTsecurity research says Thallium, which it calls a North Korean hacking group, targeted users of a private stock investment messenger service. The researchers said the motive was unclear.

AhnLab reports that Kimsuky spreads the PebbleDash backdoor mainly through spear-phishing emails with shortcut files disguised as documents. The chain then uses PowerShell, a Dropbox and TCP socket command channel, and a patched system file to get around remote desktop authentication.
Microsoft says targets get a spear-phishing PDF and are told to run attacker code in PowerShell as administrator. The code installs a browser-based remote desktop tool.

South Korea's National Cyber Security Center attributes a January 2024 supply chain attack to Kimsuky. A compromised construction trade website served trojanized security installers signed with a valid certificate.

ENKI WhiteHat attributes new Android DOCSWAP variants to Kimsuky, citing shared infrastructure, a known phishing string and Korean-language comments. It calls this strong evidence, not definitive confirmation, and could not confirm how victims were first reached.
S2W suspects a possible connection between the DocSwap mobile spyware and Kimsuky. The app logs keystrokes through accessibility services.

Breakglass Intelligence describes a three-stage chain that starts from a help file disguised as API documentation. It covers reconnaissance with scheduled-task persistence, a PowerShell bridge, and a keylogger with clipboard monitoring.

ESTsecurity researchers said Thallium altered the installer of a stock investment messaging app so that it fetched and ran a malicious script. They also described a rogue scheduled task and a remote access trojan.

Genians describes a 2026 campaign that began with reply-based spearphishing posing as a National Assembly member's aide. Later stages came from a public note service whose contents the operator swapped to change tools, including XenoRAT.
Genians says it cannot completely rule out that a third party imitated the same techniques, and that no single decisive piece of evidence was found.
Treat unexpected shortcut files, help files and Office macros with suspicion, especially when they arrive in a reply to a real conversation.
Never paste or run commands because a web page or a contact tells you to. Patch email and VPN servers promptly.
